findings.description: Pause action is hidden in the alert list view because it still requires the now-removed rulerRule. — WHAT: The Pause menu item is gated on `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)` which is `undefined` in the alert list view, so Pause is silently dropped even though the new `canPause` (grafana ability) is true. WHY: In the list view GrafanaRuleListItem only passes `promRule` (no `rulerRule`), so the Pause action regresses — it was available before this PR and now never renders. HOW: Render the pause item based on the grafana promRule path (or re-supply the ruler rule) instead of guarding on `rulerRule`; e.g. use `prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(promRule)` and a pause component that operates on the grafana identifier rather than `rulerRule`.

Delete action is hidden in the alert list view because it still requires the now-removed rulerRule. — WHAT: The Delete menu item is gated on `canDelete && rulerRule`, and `handleDelete(rulerRule, ...)` also needs the ruler rule, so Delete is silently dropped in the alert list view where `rulerRule` is undefined. WHY: Removing the ruler API from the list view leaves `rulerRule` undefined, so the Delete action regresses and users can no longer delete a rule from the list. HOW: Either keep fetching the ruler rule for delete, or construct the delete flow from the grafana `promRule`/identifier instead of requiring `rulerRule`.

Silence action in the list view is a no-op because the drawer requires the now-removed rulerRule. — WHAT: The SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer is gated on `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)`, but in the list view `rule` (rulerRule) is undefined, so the drawer never renders even though the AlertRuleMenu still shows the Silence menu item (canSilence is true from the grafana ability). WHY: Clicking "Silence notifications" in the list view sets `showSilenceDrawer` to true but nothing appears — a silent no-op and broken silence flow. HOW: Guard the silence menu item/drawer consistently, e.g. only show the silence action when a ruler rule is available, or render the drawer from the grafana promRule/identifier rather than `rule`.

Grafana recording rules lose the Export/DeletePermanently actions because ModifyExport is gated on the alerting-only type guard instead of the broader Grafana-managed guard. — WHAT: useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities gates AlertRuleAction.ModifyExport (and DeletePermanently) on isAlertingRule, which is prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) — true only for Alerting rules, not Recording rules. WHY: the previous ruler hook gated ModifyExport on isGrafanaManagedAlertRule = rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rule) (true for both alerting and recording Grafana rules), so Grafana recording rules can no longer be exported (Export menu item hidden) in the new list view. HOW: use a broad Grafana-managed check (prometheusRuleType.grafana.rule(rule)) for ModifyExport and DeletePermanently, keeping the narrower isAlertingRule only for Pause/Restore/Silence.

goldensDetail.text: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.

RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.

findings.description: Office365 credential refresh overwrites the real refresh_token with the literal 'refresh_token' when the provider omits it, breaking future refreshes. — WHAT: parseRefreshTokenResponse replaces an absent refresh_token with the literal string "refresh_token", which is then spread over and persisted as the credential's real refresh token. WHY: because refreshTokenResponseSchema marks refresh_token optional, when Microsoft's token endpoint omits it the stored credential's refresh_token is overwritten with "refresh_token", so every subsequent token refresh fails. HOW: keep the existing refresh token when the response omits it (use safeParse directly, or make the helper preserve the prior refresh_token instead of substituting a sentinel).

Salesforce refresh fetches a new access token but builds the connection with the stale stored token, making the refresh ineffective. — WHAT: the freshly fetched access token is persisted to the DB but the jsforce.Connection is still built with the stale stored credentialKey.access_token (and stale instance_url), so the refreshed token is never used. WHY: the connection operates with the old, possibly expired access token, defeating the added refresh; requests will 401 until jsforce lazily refreshes, and the new instance_url returned by Salesforce is ignored. HOW: construct the connection from the parsed refresh response (accessTokenParsed.data.access_token / instance_url) instead of credentialKey.

Webex token refresh in credential-sync mode parses the minimal sync response with the full schema, so it always fails. — WHAT: webex wraps the token fetch in refreshOAuthTokens (which in credential-sync mode returns the sync endpoint's minimal {access_token, expires_in} response) but still validates it with the full webexRefreshedTokenSchema. WHY: the sync response lacks scope/token_type/refresh_token/refresh_token_expires_in, so safeParse always fails and Webex token refresh throws 'Invalid refreshed tokens were returned' whenever credential sync is enabled. HOW: use parseRefreshTokenResponse(responseBody, webexRefreshedTokenSchema) like zoom/office365, so the minimal schema is applied in sync mode.

minimumTokenResponseSchema's computed-key trick collapses to "[object Object]" and never captures the expiry, so sync-mode token refreshes persist NaN/stale expiries. — WHAT: `minimumTokenResponseSchema` uses computed property keys (`[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]`) that both evaluate to the literal string "[object Object]", so the second key overwrites the first and the schema collapses to `{ access_token, "[object Object]"?: unknown }`; it never captures the expiry field the comment claims it does. WHY: in credential-sync mode the sync endpoint's `expires_in`/`expiry_date` is stripped by zod's default `.strip()`, so downstream adapters persist broken state — zoom computes `key.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + newTokens.expires_in * 1000)` where `newTokens.expires_in` is `undefined`, yielding `NaN` (serialized to `null` in the DB) which then fails `zoomTokenSchema.parse` on the next read, and office365 keeps the stale already-expired `expires_in`, forcing a token refresh and DB write on every subsequent call. HOW: explicitly capture the expiry and pass through the rest, e.g. `z.object({ access_token: z.string(), expires_in: z.number().optional(), expiry_date: z.number().optional() }).catchall(z.unknown())`.

Hardcoded production login.salesforce.com token URL breaks Salesforce sandbox orgs, which must refresh at test.salesforce.com. — WHAT: the refresh-token POST hardcodes the production endpoint `https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token` instead of deriving it from the credential's `instance_url`. WHY: Salesforce sandbox orgs (whose `instance_url` is `https://<name>--<sandbox>.sandbox.my.salesforce.com`) must exchange refresh tokens at `https://test.salesforce.com`; hitting the production endpoint returns `invalid_grant`, so `getClient` throws `HttpError` and the Salesforce integration breaks entirely for sandbox users. HOW: derive the login URL from `credentialKey.instance_url` (use `test.salesforce.com` when the instance URL contains "sandbox"/"my.salesforce.com"), or reuse jsforce's oauth2 refresh which resolves the correct domain.

missedGoldens.text: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should st

goldensDetail.text: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.
Invalid Zod schema syntax. Computed property keys like [z.string().toString()] are not valid in Zod object schemas and will cause runtime errors.

parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.

When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.

When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.

findings.description: Flexbox conversion drops the button's float-based right alignment, so add margin-left: auto. — WHAT: Converting `.small-action` to a flex container silently disables the `float: right` on its `button` child (floats are ignored on flex items), so the action/undo button loses its right alignment and renders inline right after the description text. WHY: The row previously relied on `float: right` to push the button to the far edge; with flexbox there is no `margin-left: auto` to compensate, producing a visible layout regression. HOW: Add `margin-left: auto` to `.small-action button` (and drop the now-dead `float: right`), or keep the button outside the flex layout.

order mixin is off-by-one between 1-based box-ordinal-group and 0-based order. — WHAT: `@mixin order` passes the same value to `-webkit-box-ordinal-group`/`-moz-box-ordinal-group` (1-based, initial value 1) and to `order` (0-based, initial value 0), which is an off-by-one. WHY: For `order(0)`/`order(1)` (or negative values) old-WebKit/Firefox will render the element in a different position than modern browsers (e.g. `order(1)` equals the default group in the old box model but sorts after defaults in modern flexbox); the current `order(2)`/`order(3)` calls happen to keep relative order, so this is latent but will mis-render as soon as the mixin is used with 0/1. HOW: Offset the legacy property by one: `-webkit-box-ordinal-group: $val + 1;` and `-moz-box-ordinal-group: $val + 1;`.

align-items mixin is missing -moz-box-align despite flexbox() emitting display: -moz-box, so 2009-Mozilla engines ignore the alignment — WHAT: the `align-items` mixin omits `-moz-box-align`, while the `flexbox()`/`inline-flex()` mixins emit `display: -moz-box`/`-moz-inline-box`. WHY: on any engine that resolves to the 2009 Mozilla box model, `@include align-items(center/baseline)` has no effect and the header/action content loses its intended vertical alignment — the mixin claims all prefixes but drops the Mozilla 2009 one. HOW: add `-moz-box-align: $alignment;` alongside `-webkit-box-align`.

missedGoldens.text: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.

goldensDetail.text: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.

findings.description: Refactor drops the traceID field from plugin request completion logs, breaking trace correlation. — WHAT: The refactored LoggerMiddleware.logRequest drops the `traceID` field that the old code explicitly appended to every "Plugin Request Completed" log line. WHY: The new ContextualLoggerMiddleware.instrumentContext only enriches the context with endpoint/pluginId/dsName/dsUID/uname, and no registered contextual log provider supplies a traceID (verified via grep of RegisterContextualLogProvider/WithContextualAttributes), so plugin request logs permanently lose trace correlation, breaking the ability to join these logs with traces. HOW: Re-add traceID to logParams via tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false) (re-importing pkg/infra/tracing), or add traceID to the contextual attributes in instrumentContext.

logRequest now silently depends on ContextualLoggerMiddleware running before LoggerMiddleware or contextual fields are lost. — WHAT: LoggerMiddleware.logRequest no longer receives pluginCtx/endpoint as arguments and derives pluginId/endpoint/dsName/dsUID/uname solely from m.logger.FromContext(ctx), which only carries those values if the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware enriched the context before LoggerMiddleware runs. WHY: In the old code these fields were always present (explicit params plus pluginCtx fields); now, if the middleware stack does not place NewContextualLoggerMiddleware before NewLoggerMiddleware (or omits it), the "Plugin Request Completed" log silently loses the plugin/endpoint/datasource/user context. I searched for the middleware wiring and found no call sites in the repo, so the ordering could not be confirmed. HOW: Verify the client middleware stack applies ContextualLoggerMiddleware upstream (outer) of LoggerMiddleware.

NewContextualLoggerMiddleware is never wired into the client middleware stack, so plugin request logs lose pluginId/endpoint/dsName/dsUID/uname that LoggerMiddleware now expects from FromContext. — WHAT: NewContextualLoggerMiddleware is added but the PR contains no wiring that registers it in the plugin client middleware chain, so the contextual log enrichment it performs is never applied. WHY: LoggerMiddleware.logRequest now obtains per-request fields via m.logger.FromContext(ctx) (logger_middleware.go:58); because MetricsMiddleware no longer calls instrumentContext and nothing adds NewContextualLoggerMiddleware to the stack, FromContext returns a logger without pluginId/endpoint/dsName/dsUID/uname, so those fields are silently dropped from every "Plugin Request Completed" log line. HOW: add NewContextualLoggerMiddleware() to the middleware stack at a position that wraps (runs before) NewLoggerMiddleware(...), e.g. append it ahead of the logger middleware when assembling the client decorator.

goldensDetail.text: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.

findings.description: Owner is stored via the Actor object's own PK (`owner.id`) rather than the resolved user/team id, and `is_user`/`is_team` may not exist on the returned object. — WHAT: `owner.id` is assigned to `owner_user_id`/`owner_team_id`, but `ActorField` returns an `Actor` object whose `id` is the actor-table primary key, not the user/team id; the code also depends on `owner.is_user`/`owner.is_team`, which are not attributes of the Actor model (it exposes `resolve()`/`type`). WHY: stores the wrong owner identifier (silently pointing ownership at an unrelated user/team whose id collides with the actor PK) or raises AttributeError at runtime when creating/updating a detector. HOW: resolve the actor to its target object, e.g. `actor_type, resolved = owner.resolve()` and use `resolved.id`, or read `owner.user_id`/`owner.team_id`, instead of `owner.id` and `is_user`/`is_team`.

Required `destination`/`attempts` fields reject working-draft reports that lack them, so only editor's-draft reports are accepted. — WHAT: `destination = serializers.CharField()` and `attempts = serializers.IntegerField(min_value=1)` are required, but the working-draft report spec (w3.org/TR/reporting-1, cited in the comment) has no `destination` or `attempts` fields — only the editor's draft does. WHY: reports from browsers implementing the working draft are rejected with 422 (`serializer.is_valid()` False), defeating the stated intent to 'support both specs'. HOW: mark both fields `required=False` (with sensible defaults) so working-draft reports are accepted.

Mutual-exclusion checks use truthiness, so a falsy-but-valid value like age=0 fails to trigger the error and both fields are accepted. — WHAT: `validate_timestamp`/`validate_age` use truthiness (`if self.initial_data.get("age")`) instead of checking key presence. WHY: `age=0` (a valid value meaning the report is 0ms old) together with a present `timestamp` evaluates falsy and skips the mutual-exclusion error, so a report with both `age` and `timestamp` is accepted despite the contract. HOW: check membership, e.g. `if "age" in self.initial_data:`.

URLField rejects valid browser reports whose url is blank or non-http (about:blank/blob:/data:/chrome-extension:), dropping them with 422. — WHAT: `url = serializers.URLField()` enforces Django's URLValidator, which only accepts absolute http/https/ftp/ftps URLs and rejects blank values. WHY: browser crash/intervention/deprecation reports commonly originate from `about:blank`, `blob:`, `data:`, or `chrome-extension:` documents (e.g., ad/sandboxed iframes, workers), so their `url` fails validation and the entire report is rejected with 422 and silently dropped; the validated `url` is never used downstream (only `type` feeds the metric), so the strict check has no compensating benefit. HOW: relax the field to `serializers.CharField()` (or a URLField with a permissive validator allowing empty and non-http schemes) since the value is only logged/forwarded and never used for routing or fetching.

findings.description: get_monitor_environment_context computes a schedule_type-displayed config copy but returns the raw config, discarding the conversion. — WHAT: get_monitor_environment_context builds a local `config` dict and replaces `schedule_type` with its human-readable display, but the returned context uses the raw `monitor_environment.monitor.config`, discarding the computed value. WHY: the `schedule_type` in the monitor context attached to the occurrence stays the raw enum/int instead of the display string, so the intended humanization is silently lost (and the `.copy()` is wasted work). Note this is a latent bug carried over verbatim from mark_failed.py, not a new regression. HOW: return the computed dict: `"config": config` instead of `"config": monitor_environment.monitor.config`.

findings.description: retryCount>1 delete branch is missing the SMS method filter, so it deletes reminders of any method. — WHAT: The `retryCount: { gt: 1 }` branch of the deleteMany OR is not scoped to `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` (unlike the first branch). WHY: it will delete reminders of any method once their retryCount exceeds 1; today only SMS reminders get retryCount written, but any future writer (EMAIL/WHATSAPP) would have its reminders silently wiped, and it is inconsistent with the first branch. HOW: add `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` (and `scheduled: false`) to the retryCount branch.

Temporary SMS-lock state returns undefined from scheduleSMS and is counted as a retryable failure, permanently deleting reminders after 2 runs. — WHAT: The `else` branch increments retryCount when `twilio.scheduleSMS` returns falsy, but scheduleSMS returns `undefined` (not an error) specifically when SMS sending is locked (`isSMSSendingLocked` -> smsLockState LOCKED). WHY: SMS lock is a temporary/admin-reversible state; a locked account now has its pending reminders permanently deleted after 2 cron runs instead of being retried until the scheduled date, losing real reminders. HOW: treat the locked/undefined result as a no-op (skip) rather than a retryable failure, or only increment retryCount on an actual thrown scheduling error.

The catch block counts any reminder-processing error (not just SMS send failures) toward retryCount, deleting reminders that never actually failed to send. — WHAT: The `catch` block increments retryCount for ANY exception in the per-reminder try block, which wraps template rendering, bookingMetadataSchema.parse, customTemplate/smsReminderTemplate, prisma.profile.findFirst, and getBookerBaseUrl — not just the SMS send call. WHY: a persistent non-SMS error (e.g. malformed booking metadata or a template error) will now increment retryCount and, after 2 runs, delete a reminder whose SMS was never actually attempted — silently dropping reminders. HOW: narrow the retryCount increment to failures from `twilio.scheduleSMS` (move the call out of the broad try, or re-throw a specific error), and keep the generic catch as log-only.

Non-atomic retryCount increment can lose updates under concurrent cron runs, so reminders may never reach the delete threshold. — WHAT: retryCount is updated with an absolute `reminder.retryCount + 1` computed from the value read at findMany time, rather than Prisma's atomic `increment: 1`. WHY: two overlapping cron invocations that read the same stale retryCount both write the same result, so a reminder can fail twice yet remain at retryCount=1 forever and never be deleted — breaking the PR's own invariant. HOW: use `data: { retryCount: { increment: 1 } }`.

goldensDetail.text: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).

The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.

findings.description: Killed/terminated flusher child processes are never joined, leaking zombie processes and resources on every restart. — WHAT: `_ensure_processes_alive` kills a multiprocessing child and immediately replaces it via `_create_process_for_shards` without ever calling `join()`/`close()` on the old process, and `join()` calls `terminate()` without joining. WHY: the killed child becomes a zombie until the parent reaps it (waitpid), leaking process handles, fds and shared-memory/semaphore objects on every unhealthy event — now multiplied across N per-shard processes, which the old single-process code only leaked once. HOW: join the killed process before recreating it (and join after terminate in `join()`).

Hung flusher threads are never killed and are replaced, leaving duplicate threads flushing the same shards. — WHAT: In the thread path (`produce_to_pipe is not None`), a hung flusher thread is never terminated because `kill()` is guarded by `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`, yet `_create_process_for_shards` still starts a replacement thread. WHY: the old hung thread keeps running and polling Redis/flushing the same shards concurrently with the new thread, causing duplicate segment production and duplicate backpressure/heartbeat writes in the test path. HOW: signal the thread to stop (e.g. a per-process stop Event checked in `main`'s loop) instead of relying on `Process.kill`, or skip the restart for non-killable threads.

Comma-joined multi-shard strings used as metric/tag values create high-cardinality tags and inconsistent tag keys. — WHAT: `shard_tag = ",".join(map(str, shards))` is used as a metric/tag value (`tags={"shard": shard_tag}`, `tags={"shards": shard_tag}`, and `sentry_sdk.set_tag("sentry_spans_buffer_shards", shard_tag)`). WHY: with round-robin shard-to-process assignment the value is a rebalance-dependent combination (e.g. "0,8,16,...") producing high-cardinality tag values across consumers, and the produce timer uses key `shard` while wait_produce uses `shards`, breaking metric grouping on the same dimension. HOW: emit one metric per shard with a scalar `shard` tag instead of a comma-joined multi-shard value, and use a consistent tag key.

Per-process SpansBuffer subsets make max-flush-segments a per-process limit, N-fold amplifying flush volume and weakening any_shard_at_limit backpressure. — WHAT: Creating `SpansBuffer(shards)` with a per-process shard subset changes `flush_segments`'s `shard_factor = max(1, len(self.assigned_shards))` from the total shard count to the subset count, so `spans.buffer.max-flush-segments` silently becomes a per-process limit instead of a per-consumer limit. WHY: with N flusher processes, the aggregate flush volume per iteration becomes ~N× `max_flush_segments` (amplifying the Redis read and Kafka produce burst), and the `any_shard_at_limit` backpressure flag (buffer.py:411, `len(segment) >= max_segments_per_shard`) now requires N× the prior per-shard backlog before triggering, weakening the Redis-overflow protection this backpressure is meant to provide. HOW: keep the per-shard cap derived from the TOTAL shard count (e.g., store `self.total_shards = len(buffer.assigned_shards)` in SpanFlusher and have `SpansBuffer`/`flush_segments` divide `max_flush_segments` by the total rather than `len(self.assigned_shards)`).

Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.

Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

findings.description: Removing the full BuildIndex mutex allows concurrent builds of the same file-backed bleve index, risking corruption/errors. — WHAT: BuildIndex no longer holds cacheMu for the duration of the build, so two concurrent getOrCreateIndex calls for the same NamespacedResource both pass the GetIndex()==nil check and build the index simultaneously. WHY: For file-backed indexes (size > FileThreshold) both goroutines call bleve.New(dir) and write to the same on-disk directory concurrently, corrupting the index or failing with 'index already open'/lock errors; previously the full-function mutex serialized these builds. HOW: Serialize builds per key (e.g. golang.org/x/sync/singleflight keyed by NamespacedResource, or re-check b.cache under the lock and hold a per-key lock while building) instead of locking only the final cache write.

TotalDocs() reads the cache map without a lock while the just-started watch goroutine can write it, causing a data race/panic. — WHAT: The newly added s.search.TotalDocs() call in init iterates bleveBackend.cache without holding the read lock, right after the watch goroutine is started. WHY: The watch goroutine calls handleEvent → getOrCreateIndex → BuildIndex, which writes b.cache[key] = idx; a concurrent unlocked map range combined with that map write triggers Go's 'concurrent map iteration and map write' fatal runtime error. HOW: Take cacheMu.RLock() inside TotalDocs(), or compute TotalDocs before starting the watch goroutine.

goldensDetail.text: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.

Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

goldensDetail.text: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.

Logical AND (`&&`) used instead of logical OR (`||`) in `isTeamAdminOrOwner` authorization check. — WHAT: `isTeamAdminOrOwner` checks `isTeamAdmin(...) && isTeamOwner(...)` with logical AND instead of logical OR.
WHY: Team owners or team admins will fail the permission check if they do not satisfy both conditions simultaneously, causing an unauthorized `FORBIDDEN` error when attempting to add guests.
HOW: Replace `&&` with `||` so that either a team admin or team owner is granted access.

findings.description:
Premature localCache insertion in tagDeviceUI allows rejected devices exceeding the device limit to authenticate on subsequent requests. — WHAT: `tagDeviceUI` caches the device ID in `localCache` before `CreateOrUpdateDevice` succeeds, without evicting it on error.

WHY: When a new device reaches `TagDevice` after the device limit is reached, `CreateOrUpdateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` and authentication is rejected. However, because `localCache` already recorded the key, the device's next request results in a cache hit in `tagDeviceUI`, which returns `nil` without calling `CreateOrUpdateDevice`, bypassing the device limit and allowing unauthorized anonymous access.

HOW: In `tagDeviceUI`, only store the key in `localCache` after `a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice(ctx, device)` succeeds, or delete the key from `localCache` if `CreateOrUpdateDevice` returns an error.

Cached device key on tagDeviceUI failure allows subsequent requests to bypass AnonymousDeviceLimit — WHAT: `tagDeviceUI` stores the device key in `localCache` before `CreateOrUpdateDevice` succeeds, but does not evict it when `CreateOrUpdateDevice` fails with `ErrDeviceLimitReached`.
WHY: When a new device is rejected after reaching `AnonymousDeviceLimit`, its device ID remains in `localCache` (29-minute TTL); any subsequent request with the same device ID hits the cache, returns `nil`, and successfully authenticates, completely bypassing the device limit.
HOW: Evict the device cache key on error (e.g. `a.localCache.Delete(taggedDevice.CacheKey())` when `err != nil`) or only store the key in `localCache` after `CreateOrUpdateDevice` succeeds.

findings.description:
Storage.Create failure records legacy duration metrics instead of storage duration metrics. — WHAT: d.recordLegacyDuration is called when d.Storage.Create returns an error.
WHY: Storage failure latency and error counts are recorded against the legacy storage histogram metric instead of the storage histogram metric, corrupting dual-writer observability.
HOW: Change d.recordLegacyDuration to d.recordStorageDuration.

Delete passes object name instead of resource kind to recordStorageDuration. — WHAT: recordStorageDuration is passed the object instance name instead of options.Kind on successful Storage.Delete.
WHY: Using instance names instead of resource kinds creates high-cardinality Prometheus labels and mismatches the kind label recorded across all other dual writer methods and error branches.
HOW: Pass options.Kind instead of name to d.recordStorageDuration.

Storage.Update failure records legacy duration metrics instead of storage duration metrics. — WHAT: d.recordLegacyDuration is called when d.Storage.Update fails.
WHY: Storage update failures and latencies are recorded against the legacy storage histogram metric instead of the storage histogram metric, distorting telemetry and alerting.
HOW: Change d.recordLegacyDuration to d.recordStorageDuration.

Async Legacy.DeleteCollection records storage duration metric instead of legacy duration metric. — WHAT: d.recordStorageDuration is called inside the async Legacy.DeleteCollection goroutine.
WHY: Asynchronous legacy delete-collection execution time and errors are recorded under the storage duration histogram rather than the legacy duration histogram.
HOW: Change d.recordStorageDuration to d.recordLegacyDuration.

findings.description:
Missing `require 'open-uri'` in `TopicEmbed.import_remote` causes `open(url)` to fail when opening HTTP/HTTPS URLs. — WHAT: `TopicEmbed.import_remote` calls `open(url)` without ensuring `open-uri` is required.
WHY: Without `open-uri` loaded, `Kernel#open` attempts to open `url` as a local filesystem path and raises `Errno::ENOENT` when fetching remote URLs.
HOW: Add `require 'open-uri'` before calling `open(url)` in `import_remote` (or require it at the top of the file).

Unchecked `i.content.scrub` raises `NoMethodError` on RSS feeds where items only define `description`. — WHAT: `i.content.scrub` is called without guarding against `nil` or falling back to `i.description`.
WHY: SimpleRSS items in RSS 2.0 feeds without `<content:encoded>` elements leave `i.content` as `nil`, causing a runtime `NoMethodError: undefined method 'scrub' for nil:NilClass` and aborting feed processing.
HOW: Fall back to `i.description` and ensure content is present before calling `.scrub`.

Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.

findings.description:
Duplicate `self.downsize` definition overwrites the 4/5-argument method signature, causing ArgumentError when invoked with separate width and height. — WHAT: Defining `self.downsize` twice in `OptimizedImage` overwrites the `(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` definition.
WHY: Ruby does not support method overloading by parameter count or type; the second definition clobbers the first, causing callers like `ResizeEmoji` (`OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, 100, 100, opts)`) to raise an `ArgumentError (wrong number of arguments)`.
HOW: Unify `self.downsize` into a single method that supports both dimension strings (`"80%"`, `"100x100"`) and separate `max_width`/`max_height` arguments.

record_for_host compares lower(host) = ? but does not normalize the parameter’s case, so mixed‑case referer hosts may fail to match even though comparison intends to be case‑insensitive.

Because this migration inserts embeddable_hosts rows with raw SQL, any existing embeddable_hosts values that include http:// or /https:// or path segments won’t go through the EmbeddableHost model’s normalization, so the new host lookup (which compares only the bare host) may fail for migrated data. Consider ensuring that migrated hosts are normalized to the same format as newly created EmbeddableHost records so existing embedding configurations keep working.

findings.description:
Missing re-check of entryPointAssetsCache under write lock causes broken double-checked locking. — WHAT: Missing check for `entryPointAssetsCache != nil` after acquiring `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()`.
WHY: When multiple concurrent requests call `GetWebAssets` on cold start, all waiting goroutines bypass the initial check and redundantly re-read from disk and re-parse the manifest sequentially instead of returning the already cached assets.
HOW: Re-check `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil` immediately after acquiring the write lock before executing the manifest loading logic.

Re-check entryPointAssetsCache under write lock to complete double-checked locking pattern — WHAT: Missing check for `entryPointAssetsCache != nil` after acquiring `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()`.
WHY: Multiple concurrent goroutines requesting assets on cold start will pass the initial RLock check and sequentially re-read and parse the manifest, doing redundant I/O and potentially overwriting a valid cache with nil if a later load fails.
HOW: Re-check `entryPointAssetsCache != nil` (when not in dev mode) immediately after acquiring `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()` and return the cached value.

missedGoldens.text: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) rega

goldensDetail.text: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.

In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

Checking response.statusText !== 'OK' instead of !response.ok can cause valid token refresh responses to throw an error. — WHAT: `response.statusText !== "OK"` is used to determine if the Salesforce token refresh request failed.
WHY: `response.statusText` is not guaranteed to be `"OK"` for successful HTTP responses (for example, in HTTP/2 where statusText is empty `""`, or if a proxy alters reason phrases), which causes successful token refresh requests to falsely throw an `HttpError`.
HOW: Check `!response.ok` instead of comparing `response.statusText` against `"OK"`.

findings.description: Client removal crashes with UnsupportedOperationException when V1+V2 features are both enabled because ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled throws — WHAT: `setPermissionsEnabled(ClientModel, boolean)` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`, but the event listener in `AdminPermissions.registerListener` (line 164) calls `management(session, realm).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false)` when a client is removed. WHY: When both `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ` (V1, gates the listener at line 150) and `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2` (V2, makes `management()` return `MgmtPermissionsV2`) are enabled, removing any client throws `UnsupportedOperationException` instead of cleaning up permissions — the crash prevents the removal event from completing. Before this PR, `MgmtPermissionsV2` did not override `clients()`, so the V1 implementation was used and worked. This PR adds `MgmtPermissionsV2.clients()` (lines 88-93) which dispatches to `ClientPermissionsV2`, where `setPermissionsEnabled` throws. HOW: Make `ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled` a no-op (or log-and-return) instead of throwing, since V2 doesn't use the V1 per-client permission model and there is nothing to clean up.

Missing null check on getResourceTypeResource result causes NPE in hasPermission(ClientModel, String) when all-clients resource doesn't exist — WHAT: `hasPermission(ClientModel, String)` calls `AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(...)` (line 217) and then immediately uses the result in `findByResource(server, resource)` (line 219) without a null check. WHY: `getResourceTypeResource` returns null when the "Clients" type resource has not been created yet in the store (or when `supportsAuthorizationSchema` returns false), causing a NullPointerException in `policyStore.findByResource(server, null)` — this would crash any `canManage`/`canView`/`canConfigure`/`canMapRoles` check for a client that has no per-client resource. HOW: Add a null check after `getResourceTypeResource` and return false, mirroring the null-safe pattern already used in `hasPermission(String scope)` (lines 244-247).

setPermissionsEnabled throws UnsupportedOperationException but is called by the ClientRemovedEvent listener when V2 is active, crashing cleanup — WHAT: `setPermissionsEnabled(ClientModel, boolean)` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`, but the event listener in `AdminPermissions.registerListener` (line 150) calls `management(...).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(cast.getClient(), false)` when `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ` is enabled — and `management()` returns `MgmtPermissionsV2` when V2 is enabled, whose `clients()` returns `ClientPermissionsV2`. WHY: When both `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ` and `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2` features are enabled, removing a client triggers the `ClientRemovedEvent` handler which calls this method and throws `UnsupportedOperationException`, crashing the event listener and preventing permission cleanup. The same issue affects `RoleRemovedEvent` and `GroupRemovedEvent` via the V2 equivalents. HOW: Either make `setPermissionsEnabled` a no-op in V2 (instead of throwing) or guard the event listener to check which V1/V2 mode is active before calling cleanup methods.

hasPermission can NPE when getResourceTypeResource returns null because there is no null check before findByResource — WHAT: `hasPermission(ClientModel, String)` at line 219 calls `authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource)` without null-checking `resource`, which can be null when `getResourceTypeResource` returns null (e.g., when the 'all-clients' resource does not exist yet or admin permissions are not fully configured for the realm). WHY: If the per-client resource lookup fails (line 214-215 returns null) and the fallback `getResourceTypeResource` also returns null, the `findByResource` call at line 219 will throw a NullPointerException, causing all permission checks for that client to fail with a server error rather than returning false. HOW: Add a null check on `resource` after the `getResourceTypeResource` call, returning false if null, mirroring the guard pattern already used for `server == null`.

goldensDetail.text: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.

findings.description: isTeamAdminOrOwner uses && instead of ||, blocking team admins from adding guests — WHAT: `isTeamAdminOrOwner` uses `&&` between `isTeamAdmin` and `isTeamOwner`, but `isTeamOwner` is a strict subset of `isTeamAdmin` (OWNER implies ADMIN), so the expression collapses to `isTeamOwner` only. WHY: Team admins (role=ADMIN, not OWNER) are blocked from adding guests even though the variable name and intent indicate both admins and owners should be allowed — they get a FORBIDDEN error. HOW: Change `&&` to `||`.

sendAddGuestsEmails receives original guests array instead of filtered uniqueGuests, sending notifications to existing attendees — WHAT: `sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` passes the original `guests` array instead of `uniqueGuests`, which excludes existing attendees and blacklisted emails. WHY: `sendAddGuestsEmails` uses the second argument to determine which attendees receive the 'new guests added' notification (email-manager.ts line 541: `if (newGuests.includes(attendee.email))`), so existing attendees whose emails appear in the original `guests` list will receive spurious notification emails even though they were not newly added. HOW: Pass `uniqueGuests` instead of `guests`.

Blacklist bypass via case mismatch — guest emails are not lowercased before comparison against the lowercased blacklist — WHAT: The blacklist comparison `!blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)` does not lowercase `guest` before comparing, while `blacklistedGuestEmails` are explicitly lowercased. WHY: A blacklisted email like `admin@example.com` can be bypassed by submitting `Admin@Example.com` — the `includes` check fails because the case differs, allowing the blacklisted guest to be added to the booking. HOW: Lowercase `guest` before comparison: `!blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest.toLowerCase())`.

Input array is not deduplicated before createMany, allowing duplicate attendee records — WHAT: `uniqueGuests` filter only removes emails already in `booking.attendees` and blacklisted emails, but does not deduplicate within the input `guests` array. The Attendee Prisma model has no `@@unique([bookingId, email])` constraint, so `createMany` creates duplicate attendee records when the input contains the same email twice.

WHY: Passing `guests: ["a@b.com", "a@b.com"]` creates two identical Attendee rows for the same booking, causing duplicate calendar invites and emails.

HOW: Deduplicate the input before filtering: `const uniqueGuests = [...new Set(guests)].filter(...)`.

EventManager uses requesting user's credentials instead of booking organizer's, breaking calendar updates when a non-organizer team admin adds guests — WHAT: `EventManager` is initialized with `ctx.user`'s credentials and identity instead of the booking organizer's. The booking query at lines 35-39 fetches `booking.user.credentials` (organizer's credentials) but these are never used — line 158 calls `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` and line 160-163 spreads `user` (ctx.user) into EventManager.

WHY: When a team admin/owner who is NOT the organizer adds guests, `updateCalendarAttendees` attempts to update the calendar event using the admin's calendar credentials, which don't have access to the organizer's calendar — the calendar update silently fails or throws.

HOW: Use the organizer's credentials and identity: `const eventManager = new EventManager({ ...booking.user, credentials: booking.user?.credentials ?? [] })`.

goldensDetail.text: Case sensitivity bypass in email blacklist

The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.
This calls the email sender with the original guests, so existing attendees included in the input will be treated as new when sending notifications, leading to incorrect emails.

uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.
Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.

findings.description: ErrDeviceLimitReached from updateDevice fails the entire anonymous authentication, blocking new visitors from accessing Grafana once the device limit is reached. — WHAT: When the device limit is reached, a new anonymous device whose device_id is not in the DB causes updateDevice to return ErrDeviceLimitReached (rowsAffected == 0), which Authenticate propagates as a return error — failing the entire anonymous authentication. WHY: Any new anonymous visitor is blocked from accessing Grafana once the configured device limit is full, instead of simply not being tracked. This is almost certainly not the intended behavior of a device-tracking limit. HOW: In client.go, do not return ErrDeviceLimitReached from Authenticate — treat it as a non-fatal tracking failure (log and continue), the same way other TagDevice errors are handled. The limit should only prevent new device records from being created, not deny anonymous access.

Moving TagDevice from an async goroutine to the synchronous auth path adds DB latency to every anonymous request. — WHAT: TagDevice is now called synchronously on the request context instead of in a fire-and-forget goroutine, blocking authentication on DB I/O for every anonymous request. WHY: Every anonymous page load now waits for at least one CountDevices query plus an INSERT/UPDATE roundtrip before authentication completes, adding material latency to a high-frequency hot path that was previously non-blocking. HOW: Either revert to asynchronous execution (goroutine with context.Background and timeout) for the tracking side-effect, or ensure the device-limit check and write are cached/fast enough to not block the auth path.

TOCTOU race between CountDevices and INSERT allows concurrent requests to exceed the configured device limit. — WHAT: The device-limit enforcement in CreateOrUpdateDevice uses a check-then-act pattern (CountDevices then INSERT) with no transaction or lock, so concurrent requests can both pass the count < limit check and both INSERT, exceeding the configured limit. WHY: Under concurrent anonymous traffic, the device count can exceed the configured limit because the count check and the insert are not atomic. HOW: Wrap the count check and insert in a single transaction with an appropriate isolation level, or enforce the limit with a conditional INSERT guarded by a unique constraint and a count subquery.

goldensDetail.text: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.

Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.

This call won’t compile: dbSession.Exec(args...) is given a []interface{} where the first element is the query, but Exec’s signature requires a first parameter of type string (not an interface{} splat).
Returning ErrDeviceLimitReached when no rows were updated is misleading; the device might not exist.

findings.description: Create error path records storage failure under legacy metrics histogram instead of storage metrics — WHAT: Create's storage error path calls `recordLegacyDuration` instead of `recordStorageDuration`, recording a storage failure under the legacy metrics histogram. WHY: Storage Create failures will be observed as legacy duration metrics, corrupting observability dashboards and making it impossible to distinguish storage failures from legacy failures. HOW: Change `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` to `d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` to match Delete (line 103) and DeleteCollection (line 156).

Update error path records storage failure under legacy metrics histogram instead of storage metrics — WHAT: Update's storage error path calls `recordLegacyDuration` instead of `recordStorageDuration`, recording a storage failure under the legacy metrics histogram. WHY: Storage Update failures will be observed as legacy duration metrics, corrupting observability dashboards and making it impossible to distinguish storage failures from legacy failures. HOW: Change `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` to `d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` to match Delete (line 103) and DeleteCollection (line 156).

DeleteCollection async goroutine records legacy operation under storage metrics histogram instead of legacy metrics — WHAT: DeleteCollection's async legacy goroutine calls `recordStorageDuration` instead of `recordLegacyDuration`, recording a legacy operation's duration under the storage metrics histogram. WHY: Legacy DeleteCollection durations will be observed as storage metrics, corrupting observability dashboards. The goroutine performs `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` with `startLegacy` as the start time, confirming intent was to record legacy duration. HOW: Change `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)` to `d.recordLegacyDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)` to match Create (line 56), Delete (line 113), and Update (line 140).

Delete uses base logger d.Log instead of configured log for context, losing structured logging values in async goroutine — WHAT: Delete uses `d.Log` (base logger without structured values) instead of `log` (the logger configured with kind/name/method via WithValues) when creating the context. WHY: The async legacy Delete goroutine (line 112) receives this context, so any logging inside `d.Legacy.Delete` will lack the kind/name/method structured context that all other methods provide, making it harder to correlate legacy delete logs. HOW: Change `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)` to `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, log)` to match every other method in this file.

Delete success path passes object name instead of resource kind to metrics, creating inconsistent label values between success and error paths — WHAT: Delete's success path passes `name` (the object name, e.g. "my-dashboard") instead of `options.Kind` (the resource kind) to `recordStorageDuration`, while the error path (line 103) correctly passes `options.Kind`. WHY: The metric label is "kind" (metrics.go:76), so passing the object name creates inconsistent label cardinality — success metrics are recorded under the object name while error metrics are recorded under the resource kind, splitting the same operation across unrelated label values. HOW: Change `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` to `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` to match the error path and all other methods.

Async legacy-write goroutines use the request context as parent for the timeout, so the legacy writes get cancelled when the request completes instead of running for up to 10 seconds. — WHAT: The async legacy-write goroutine in Create (and identically in Delete line 145, Update line 170, DeleteCollection line 198) uses the request context `ctx` as the parent for `context.WithTimeoutCause`, so the 10-second timeout is a child of the request context. WHY: Go's net/http cancels the request context when the HTTP handler returns; that cancellation propagates to the child context and aborts the legacy write almost immediately — defeating the entire purpose of mode 3's async legacy writes as a safety measure. HOW: Detach from the request context before applying the timeout, e.g. `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(context.WithoutCancel(ctx), time.Second*10, errors.New("legacy create timeout"))` (Go 1.21+) or use `context.Background()` with a fresh timeout and carry over only the klog logger via `klog.NewContext`.

goldensDetail.text: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
Bug: calling recordLegacyDuration when storage operation fails should be recordStorageDuration.
Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.

findings.description: Stored XSS: unescaped user-controlled embed_url is injected into a raw_html post and rendered with `raw`. — WHAT: User-controlled embed_url is interpolated into HTML without escaping and stored as a raw_html post (cook_method bypasses sanitization), then rendered with `raw`. WHY: An attacker submits embed_url=`https:///x'onclick='alert(1)` — the single quote is a valid URI char so URI(...).host still matches embeddable_host, the host-only check in TopicRetriever passes, and the quote breaks out of the `href='...'` attribute in the imported footer, executing JavaScript in viewers' browsers (stored XSS in the Discourse origin inside the embeddable iframe). HOW: HTML-escape the url when interpolating: `#{CGI.escapeHTML(url)}`.

nil feed item content raises NoMethodError, aborting processing of all remaining feed items. — WHAT: `i.content.scrub` raises NoMethodError when a feed item has no content element. WHY: SimpleRSS returns nil for `content` on RSS 2.0 feeds that only expose `<description>` (no `content:encoded`); nil.scrub raises inside `rss.items.each`, aborting the entire loop so all remaining feed items are skipped, and with `sidekiq_options retry: false` (line 12) the job fails silently until the next hourly run. HOW: Guard nil/blank content before processing, e.g. `next if i.content.blank?` or fall back to `i.description`.

Protocol-relative URLs (//host) are incorrectly rewritten as root-relative paths, breaking links/images. — WHAT: `start_with?('/')` also matches protocol-relative URLs (`//cdn.com/x`), which are then mangled into `https://<embeddablehost>/cdn.com/x`. WHY: `sub(/^\/+/, '')` strips ALL leading slashes, so `//cdn.com/img.png` becomes `cdn.com/img.png` and is prefixed with the embeddable host, producing a broken link/image for any protocol-relative URL in imported content. HOW: Exclude protocol-relative URLs from the rewrite: `href.start_with?('/') && !href.start_with?('//')`.

Non-atomic check-then-create in TopicEmbed.import races between the hourly poll_feed job and retrieve_topic jobs, creating duplicate topics/embeds for the same URL. — WHAT: TopicEmbed.import performs a non-atomic check-then-create: it reads `embed = TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url).first` then, if blank, creates a topic+post+TopicEmbed inside a transaction with no locking. WHY: Two concurrent callers reaching import with the same URL — the hourly scheduled Jobs::PollFeed (poll_feed.rb:36) and a Jobs::RetrieveTopic fired by EmbedController#best via TopicRetriever#import_remote (topic_retriever.rb:52) — both pass the embed.blank? check and both create duplicate topics/posts/embeds (or one raises ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique inside the transaction with no rescue, since no unique-index error handling exists). The `exists?` guard in perform_retrieve (topic_retriever.rb:37) is itself a separate TOCTOU check and does not close the window. HOW: Guard the lookup-then-create atomically, e.g. `TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url).first_or_create!` semantics inside the transaction, or wrap with an advisory lock / `with_lock` keyed on embed_url, and rescue RecordNotUnique to re-fetch the existing embed.

findings.description: Race condition in backup code consumption allows a used code to be reused under concurrent login requests — WHAT: Backup code consumption uses a non-atomic read-modify-write — the encrypted array is decrypted, a code is null'd, and the whole array is re-encrypted and written back without any locking or optimistic concurrency check. WHY: Two concurrent login requests using different backup codes both read the original array, each nulls a different index, and the second write overwrites the first — re-enabling the first request's code and allowing it to be reused, breaking the one-time-use guarantee. HOW: Use a database transaction with a row lock (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) or an atomic update that checks the encrypted value hasn't changed since the read (optimistic concurrency).

onEnable() callback is not called if user dismisses dialog during the backup codes display step — WHAT: The PR replaced the immediate onEnable() call with setStep(SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes), deferring onEnable() to the Close button's onClick handler — but if the user dismisses the dialog via onOpenChange (Escape key or clicking outside), onEnable() is never called. WHY: 2FA has already been enabled server-side by the enable() API call, but the parent component's state is not updated, leaving the settings UI showing "Enable 2FA" instead of "Disable 2FA" until a manual page refresh. HOW: Call onEnable() in the onOpenChange handler when the step is DisplayBackupCodes, or move the onEnable() call to a useEffect that triggers when the dialog closes during that step.

resetState() doesn't revoke object URL or clear backup codes state, causing memory leak — WHAT: resetState() clears password, errorMessage, and step but does not revoke the backupCodesUrl object URL or clear backupCodes/dataUri/secret state. WHY: Each call to URL.createObjectURL creates a persistent memory reference; without revocation in resetState(), the URL leaks when the modal is closed and reopened without going through setup again. HOW: Add URL.revokeObjectURL(backupCodesUrl) and clear backupCodes, backupCodesUrl, dataUri, and secret in resetState().

JSON.parse of decrypted backup codes has no error handling, crashes on key rotation or corrupted data — WHAT: JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...)) is called without a try-catch on the decrypted backup codes in both the login authorize() and the disable endpoint. WHY: If the CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY changes between write and read (key rotation), or the stored data is corrupted, symmetricDecrypt produces garbage and JSON.parse throws an unhandled exception — in the login flow this surfaces as a generic InternalServerError, and in the disable endpoint it crashes the API handler with a 500. HOW: Wrap the JSON.parse in a try-catch that throws ErrorCode.MissingBackupCodes or ErrorCode.InternalServerError.

goldensDetail.text: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.

Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.

findings.description: ANY(${array}) in Prisma.sql may not correctly serialize JS arrays as PostgreSQL array parameters, causing runtime SQL errors — WHAT: JS arrays are passed directly to PostgreSQL's `ANY()` function via `Prisma.sql` template interpolation (`ANY(${teamIds})`, `ANY(${uniqueUserIds})`, `ANY(${userIdsFromTeam})`), but Prisma's query engine may not correctly serialize JS arrays as PostgreSQL array parameters for use with `ANY()`. WHY: When `getBaseConditions()` is eventually used in a `$queryRaw` call with "org" or "team" scope and multiple teams/users, the query could fail with a type mismatch or syntax error at runtime; the integration tests only compare `Prisma.Sql` objects and never execute the SQL, so this would not be caught. HOW: Use `Prisma.join()` for array interpolation, e.g. `Prisma.sql\`("teamId" IN (${Prisma.join(teamIds)})) AND ("isTeamBooking" = true)\`` or `Prisma.sql\`("teamId" = ANY(ARRAY[${Prisma.join(teamIds)}]::int[])) AND ("isTeamBooking" = true)\``.

Address the `ANY()` usage with JS arrays in raw SQL. — `ANY()` with JS arrays: The existing finding regarding the use of `ANY()` with JS arrays in the raw SQL conversion is explicitly referenced in the analysis. Ensure that `ANY()` is used correctly with Postgres arrays or replaced with an `IN` clause.

goldensDetail.text: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.

findings.description: Dataclass default `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is evaluated once at class definition time, giving all instances the same stale timestamp — WHAT: The `queued` field uses `timezone.now` as a direct default value, which is evaluated once at class definition time (import time) and shared across all instances. WHY: Every `AssignmentSource` created via `from_integration()` gets the same frozen timestamp — the time the module was first imported — instead of the actual time the assignment was queued, making the field semantically incorrect for all instances created after process start. HOW: Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` from `dataclasses` so a fresh timestamp is generated per instance.

findings.description: MetricAlertDetectorHandler is uninstantiable because it extends StatefulDetectorHandler without implementing any of its 5 abstract methods — WHAT: `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` was changed from extending `DetectorHandler` (with `evaluate` implemented) to extending `StatefulDetectorHandler` with just `pass`, but `StatefulDetectorHandler` has 5 abstract methods (`counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, `build_occurrence_and_event_data`, inherited `evaluate`) — none of which are implemented. WHY: When a detector with type `metric_alert_fire` is processed, `Detector.detector_handler` calls `group_type.detector_handler(self)` which tries to instantiate `MetricAlertDetectorHandler`, raising `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class` and crashing the detector processing path. The previous code implemented `evaluate` and extended `DetectorHandler` (only 1 abstract method), so it was instantiable. HOW: Either implement all abstract methods in `MetricAlertDetectorHandler`, or keep it extending `DetectorHandler` with the stub `evaluate` until the full stateful detector implementation is ready.

MetricAlertDetectorHandler cannot be instantiated because it extends StatefulDetectorHandler without implementing any of its 5 abstract methods — WHAT: `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` was changed from extending `DetectorHandler` (with `evaluate` implemented) to extending `StatefulDetectorHandler` with a `pass` body, but `StatefulDetectorHandler` has 5 abstract methods (`evaluate`, `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, `build_occurrence_and_event_data`) that are not implemented. WHY: When `Detector.detector_handler` (model line 86) calls `group_type.detector_handler(self)` to instantiate this class, Python's `abc.ABC` raises `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class` — crashing any detector processing path for detectors with type "metric_alert_fire". The old class was instantiable because it implemented `evaluate`; the new class is not. HOW: Either keep `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` extending `DetectorHandler` until the abstract methods are implemented, or provide stub implementations for all abstract methods (returning empty/no-op values as the old `evaluate` did).

findings.description: Duplicate downsize method definition overrides the 4-arg version, breaking resize_emoji.rb which still calls it with 4 args. — WHAT: The diff defines self.downsize twice — line 145 with (from, to, max_width, max_height, opts) and line 149 with (from, to, dimensions, opts) — and Ruby silently keeps only the last definition, so the surviving method takes 3 positional args. WHY: The existing caller app/jobs/regular/resize_emoji.rb:14 invokes OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, 100, 100, opts) with the old 4-arg signature, which now raises ArgumentError: wrong number of arguments (given 5, expected 4) on every emoji resize job. HOW: Remove the duplicate 4-arg definition (line 145) and update resize_emoji.rb to pass a dimensions string, e.g. OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, "100x100", opts), or keep one downsize that accepts both by normalizing width/height into a dimensions string.

Hardcoding 10MB for all upload types ignores per-type size settings and produces wrong 413 error messages for attachments. — WHAT: The client-side size check hardcodes maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 for every file type, discarding Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], and the 413 error branch hardcodes max_image_size_kb even for attachment failures. WHY: When an admin configures max_attachment_size_kb below 10MB, the client no longer rejects oversized attachments up front (server 413 / validator becomes the only gate), and the 413 message quotes the image limit rather than the attachment limit — a wrong/misleading error and a UX regression. HOW: Restore the per-type lookup for the pre-check (var maxSizeKB = Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'];) and in the 413 branch use the setting matching the uploaded type.

Duplicate `downsize` definition shadows the 5-arg version, causing ArgumentError when called with 5 positional args. — Duplicate `downsize` definition (optimized_image.rb:145 & :149) — Ruby keeps the last definition (4-arg), shadowing the 5-arg version. Traced caller resize_emoji.rb:14 which calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, 100, 100, opts)` with 5 positional args → ArgumentError at runtime. The controller's new call (line 106) uses 3 positional + opts hash, matching the surviving 4-arg definition, so it works. Already captured in existing findings.

Client-side file size check hardcoded to 10MB instead of using site settings, causing client/server mismatch. — Hardcoded 10MB in JS utilities — client-side check now uses `10 * 1024` for all file types instead of `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`. For attachment uploads, the server doesn't auto-downsize, so the client allows 10MB but the server still enforces `max_attachment_size_kb`. Already captured in existing findings.

The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.

Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).

Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.

findings.description: update and destroy crash with NoMethodError when the host id does not exist because the nil result of where(...).first is used without a guard. — WHAT: update and destroy call EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first which returns nil when no record matches, then operate on nil without a guard. WHY: save_host(nil) executes nil.host = params[:embeddable_host][:host] and destroy executes nil.destroy, both raising NoMethodError and returning a 500 instead of a clean 404/error when an admin references a non-existent or already-deleted host id. HOW: guard for nil before calling save_host/destroy and return an error response.

record_for_host lowercases the stored column but not the query parameter, so referer hosts with uppercase letters fail to match a configured host. — WHAT: record_for_host compares lower(host) on the stored column against the raw uri.host query parameter without downcasing the parameter. WHY: the before_validation callback strips scheme/path but does not normalize case, and the validation regex is case-insensitive (/i) so mixed-case hosts can be persisted; when a referer host retains uppercase letters (Ruby URI.parse preserves host case), lower(stored) = 'Example.com' fails to match a configured 'example.com', causing host_allowed? to reject a legitimately configured embed host. HOW: downcase the query parameter to match the lowercased column: where("lower(host) = ?", host.downcase).first.

destroy action references undefined success_json helper, causing NoMethodError (500) on every successful destroy. — WHAT: the destroy action renders `success_json`, a helper that is not defined anywhere in the codebase (repo-wide grep for `def success_json` and all `success_json` usages returns only this single line; application_controller.rb defines no such method). WHY: after `host.destroy` succeeds, evaluating the undefined `success_json` raises NoMethodError, so every successful destroy returns a 500 instead of a success response (the record is already deleted by then). HOW: replace with an explicit hash, e.g. `render json: { success: 'ok' }`, or define `success_json` in the base controller.

before_validation calls sub! on a possibly-nil host, raising NoMethodError instead of a clean validation error when the host param is missing. — WHAT: the before_validation callback calls `self.host.sub!(...)` with no nil guard, but `host` can be nil when the `embeddable_host[host]` param is omitted (save_host assigns `host.host = params[:embeddable_host][:host]`, which is nil for a missing key). WHY: `nil.sub!` raises NoMethodError during `host.save`, so the controller's `if host.save ... else render_json_error(host)` never reaches the clean validation-error branch — a bad/missing host param produces a 500 crash instead of a 400 validation error. HOW: coerce or guard before mutating, e.g. `self.host = self.host.to_s` or `return if self.host.blank?` at the top of the callback.

goldensDetail.text: NoMethodError before_validation in EmbeddableHost

The update and destroy methods in Admin::EmbeddableHostsController do not validate the existence of the EmbeddableHost record retrieved by ID. If EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first returns nil (i.e., the host does not exist), attempting to call methods on the nil object (e.g., save_host or destroy) will result in a NoMethodError.
record_for_host compares lower(host) = ? but does not normalize the parameter’s case, so mixed‑case referer hosts may fail to match even though comparison intends to be case‑insensitive.

Because this migration inserts embeddable_hosts rows with raw SQL, any existing embeddable_hosts values that include http:// or /https:// or path segments won’t go through the EmbeddableHost model’s normalization, so the new host lookup (which compares only the bare host) may fail for migrated data. Consider ensuring that migrated hosts are normalized to the same format as newly created EmbeddableHost records so existing embedding configurations keep working.

findings.description: Broken uniq in fallback list: locale left as String while others are Symbols, so dedup fails for anonymous users and causes double locale loading + dead fallback lookups. — WHAT: FallbackLocaleList#[] calls `.to_sym` on SiteSetting.default_locale but not on `locale`, so when I18n.locale is a String (anonymous users get `I18n.locale = SiteSetting.default_locale`, a String from LocaleSiteSetting) the `[locale, default_locale.to_sym, :en].uniq` does not dedup ("en" != :en), yielding e.g. ["en", :en]. WHY: ensure_loaded! then loads the same locale yml twice (translate_accelerator keys @loaded_locales by exact object, "en" and :en are distinct) and the string fallback entry always misses the symbol-keyed backend, adding a guaranteed-miss lookup on every cache-miss translate for all anonymous traffic. HOW: sym the locale too — `[locale.to_sym, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en].uniq.compact`.

findings.description: Inverted slug condition creates orgs with no slug when billing is disabled and redundant slug+requestedSlug when enabled — WHAT: The slug condition was inverted — `IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {}` sets slug when billing is enabled and omits it when disabled, which is the opposite of the original `!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug }`. WHY: When `IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED` is false (e.g., self-hosted instances), the organization is created with no slug at all, breaking subdomain-based routing; when it is true, both `slug` and `requestedSlug` are set simultaneously, defeating the approval/billing flow that `requestedSlug` was designed for. HOW: Restore the original condition polarity: `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})` for the slug field, keeping `requestedSlug` under the `IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED` branch.
